abstract:
The rise of big data surveillance and predictive analytics has transformed the capabilities of law enforcement and created new forms of big data policing. Police departments (P.D.s) have increasingly used algorithms to analyze massive amounts of information in order to forecast and investigate potential criminal activity, such as Chicago P.D.’s Strategic Subject List (SSL). State governments have also adopted surveillance technologies such as facial recognition and acoustic sensors in their crime-reduction efforts. This has raised many concerns about individuals’ constitutional rights of privacy, as well as the adverse impacts on marginalized communities.

More alarming, however, is the role of data brokers in allowing law enforcement agencies to not be held liable for these violations. These for-profit companies aggregate individuals’ personal data and sell it to the largest bidders. This is not only concerning but also unconstitutional as these purchases bypass the Fourth Amendment through the third-party doctrine. Yet, Congress has still not passed a federal data privacy law addressing these loopholes.

As such, this paper explores the impacts of predictive policing programs and argues for the necessity of policy intervention on data brokers in three parts. First, it provides an overview of big data policing and its evolution in light of new predictive technologies. Second, it analyzes how predictive policing challenges the constitutional protections under the Fourth Amendment and the role that commercial data brokers play in this process. Finally, the paper concludes by highlighting the need for new legislative solutions to maintain these protections and regulate the data brokerage industry.

Mary Shelley put pen to paper to write Frankenstein (1818) at the height of the British Abolitionist Movement, after the end of the slave trade, but before the abolition of slavery.1 From her mother, Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), she inherited her feminist legacy and her education. To quote Wollstonecraft, Shelley learned:

Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience; but as blind obedience is ever sought for by power, tyrants and sensualists are in the right when they endeavor to keep women in the dark, because the former only wants slaves, and the latter play things.2

The language of enslavement and empire is laced throughout Wollstonecraft's essays on female rights as she condemns society that relegates women to the position of slaves. Thus Frankenstein emerges—a joint abolitionist and feminist outcry against societal degradation. But since its publication, several disappointing adaptations have come into being that, rather than doing justice to Shelley's acute social critique, erase it. However, Nick Dear's 2012 stage adaptation seeks to undo nearly a century of lacking adaptations that erase the Creature as an intelligent

being and revives Shelley's feminist and abolitionist rhetorical throughline. In this paper, I posit that Nick Dear's adaptation of Frankenstein intentionally exacerbates the male-female binary, and inextricably links feminist and post-colonial readings of Mary Shelley's original novel through the corruption of G.W.F. Hegel's Master-Slave Dialectic. The play examines the source and implications of the Creature's desire to be acknowledged as not only a being, but as Victor Frankenstein's example of a man— a "male mother" and a conqueror.

abstract: This paper intends to use commentary from Marlon James’s A Brief History of Seven Killings to evaluate the representation of Jamaica in Rolling Stone magazine, particularly as it pertains to the Jamaican politics of 1970. The rising popularity of Rolling Stone corresponds to a significant amount of pop-cultural influence over the American public; the perception of Jamaica in America can be largely attributed to the magazine at this time. This makes representation significant, for the sake of Jamaica being appropriately presented to magazine consumers. Literary analysis of these articles shows a significant level of racism, infantilization, and exoticization of Jamaica, at the fault of reckless writing from Rolling Stone.

abstract: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH) is an adverse side effect of chronic opioid use characterized by a heightened sensitization towards pain. While the mechanisms behind OIH are still yet to be understood, many existing studies point to the neuroplasticity of the central glutaminergic system as a likely cause. Current treatment regimens remain limited and often lead to exacerbated hyperalgesic effects or even risks of overdose. In order to mitigate OIH and prevent the loss of opioid efficacy, we propose deep brain stimulation (DBS) as a potential treatment option. DBS is a procedure that targets specific areas of the brain using electrodes and has proven effective for treating various neurological movement disorders and, more recently, chronic pain. Recent experimental data has shown that DBS can alleviate aversive events in the lateral habenula (LHb), an area of the brain that is linked to reward-negative events such as depression, pain, and anxiety. In this review, we will first introduce DBS in its clinical and preclinical uses and discuss its potential as a treatment for OIH. We will then analyze the opioid epidemic, as well as how the neurocircuits of LHb may contribute to the symptoms of this global crisis. Despite the gaps in knowledge that remain about the exact mechanisms, DBS to treat OIH is a novel idea that may be very effective. This review will conclude by projecting future directions for research that can help further improve our understanding of this subject.

Prevalence of fake news has skyrocketed in recent years, tripling in frequency from 2016 to 2017. Recent research has investigated potential predictors of fake news susceptibility, such as political affiliation and news literacy. This study built off of those ideas, further investigating the political and social-media-usage patterns in fake news identification performance. Overall, we expected political extremism, mode of news ingestion, confidence, and news literacy to be moderate predictors of fake news susceptibility. We predicted that higher levels of liberal extremism, as well as increased reliance on social media for news, decreased a person’s ability to identify news as real and fake. Survey answers of 62 liberal Northwestern undergraduate students were analyzed to examine any correlations. The results indicated that liberal extremism did not significantly predict news identification performance, while social media usage significantly predicted news identification performance. In addition, social media usage significantly predicted the degree of liberal extremism, linking the previous two findings together. Our results suggested fake news susceptibility can be predicted by examining social media usage for news along with extremism in liberal beliefs. This is practically significant for all news outlets catering to more politically extreme people; news outlets should carefully tailor each headline to minimize deception and disinformation on an already fake news susceptible population. With this knowledge, educational programs in fake news identification can also be implemented to increase awareness among the American public.

Agricultural and biotechnology research scientists have asserted genetically modified (GM) foods offer immense financial, health, and environmental benefits to society, but the implementa- tion of such benefits greatly depends on public acceptance of this genetic technology (Fernbach). Widespread opposition and concern towards GM foods raise questions about the public’s understanding of GM foods and biotechnology processes in general. Therefore, the complicated interrelation between the specific variables knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes towards GM foods demands evaluation. To better understand this relationship, a detailed survey containing two distinct sections measuring knowledge of biotechnology, both self-assessed and objective, and attitudes towards GM foods was distributed to a sample of 32 high school students at Community School of Naples (CSN) in Southwest Florida. Specifically, simple random sampling was completed with the use of an online random number generator. Responses from the distributed questionnaire were critically analyzed with MiniTab statistical software. Statistically significant results show that as CSN students’ opposition to GM foods increases, scores measuring objective knowledge of biotechnology linearly decrease (correlation coefficient (r)=-0.763). Within a real- life context, this research provides insight into a notable factor (lack of knowledge of biotechnology) not only driving CSN high school students’ widespread opposition to GM foods but also potentially the general public’s opposition. The results of this research could directly aid to implement change to increase high school students’ knowledge of biotechnology, such as through curriculum adjustments in biology courses, in order to consequently achieve lower opposition and greater acceptance of GM foods in society.

This study investigates how former President Donald Trump’s “China Virus” rhetoric on Twitter impacted public online behavior by analyzing 632 related tweets and corresponding Google and YouTube searches in 2020. Key findings indicate a significant positive correlation between Trump’s use of politicized framing and an upsurge in related Google Trends, highlighting the immediate influence of political rhetoric on public online behavior.

The study controlled for U.S. and China COVID-19 death rates and Trump’s approval ratings to enhance the regression and marginal effects analysis. Results show a diminishing effect of Trump’s xenophobic influence over time. This trend suggests that growing public desensitization and an enhanced understanding of the pandemic could weaken the impact of elite xenophobic rhetoric. The analysis demonstrates the dynamic interplay between political communication and public response, highlighting the influential role of political leaders in shaping public discourse through social media.

The synthesis and characterization of a gadolinium-based contrast agent conjugated to 3-phosphoglycerate (Gd-3PG) are reported. The synthetic steps are optimized to incorporate a selective deprotection strategy for a primary tert-butyl dimethyl silyl (TBS) hydroxyl over a secondary one. The relaxivity of Gd-3PG shows characteristic improvement, likely due to secondary sphere effects and/or an increase in molecular weight (5.39 ± 0.14 mM−1 s−1 at 1.4 T and 37 °C). Michaelis–Menten enzymatic kinetics was measured on the modified 3PG-arm and it showed similar activity to the native 3PG metabolite, Km = 240 ± 30 µM. This agent and future versions of this type of GBCA, which are conjugated to glycolytic metabolites, were designed to monitor in vivo allosteric regulatory events in glycolytic processes.

abstract: The Local Bubble (LB) contains significant internal structure, including many partially ionized interstellar clouds. Some of the clouds in the vicinity of the Local Bubble have extreme properties as traced by neutral hydrogen (HI) absorption measurements towards pulsars. By observing time variability of HI absorption profiles it was suggested that some of the HI structures have high density and pressures, data representative of the tiny scale atomic structure (TSAS). However, the exact location of these structures are unknown and understanding their origin in the framework of LB formation and evolution has been impossible. We use three-dimensional dust maps (Edenhofer et al. 2023) to extract density profiles of the hydrogen volume density along the line-of-sight (LOS) to four selected pulsars. High correlation of the density profile ”peaks” to the Gaussian components of the absorption spectra as measured by Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) reveal potential 3D ”structures” that may correspond to warm neutral medium and/or cold netural medium. Column density images and analysis of dusty structures along the LOS using Glue reveal the structural and intrinsic properties of interstellar matter (ISM). Using the calculations of mean and maximum density along the LOS, we derive the ionization fraction and thermal pressure to characterize the properties of the ISM as traced by the pulsars. Our method of using absorption data in conjunction with three-dimensional dust data holds potential for broader applications, especially to validate the structures and properties of dust clouds in the LB and beyond.

Background: Maternal morbidity rates and high rates of risky obstetric interventions remain a problem in the United States. Birth doulas are a suggested solution to mitigate obstetric interventions. Despite women of different maternal ages facing different risks during pregnancy, research is not yet conclusive on whether the benefits of doulas may vary for different age groups.

Methods: A literature review was conducted through PubMed and CINAHL with the inclusion criteria that the article be published in English between 2000-2025, be about doula care and its impact on cesarean sections and/or forceps-assisted deliveries, and include age as a measured demographic. Articles must be from peer-reviewed journals. Literature regarding forceps-assisted deliveries were parsed out.

Findings: Doulas likely reduce the risk of cesarean sections for adolescents (<20) by connecting adolescents with needed resources and reducing stress. Stronger evidence exists showing doulas reduce cesarean section rates for adults (20-34) by screening for maternal mental health, assisting mothers in accessing needed resources, and providing culturally competent care. Inconclusive literature was identified for pregnant people in the advanced age group (35+).

Conclusion: Existing literature has the strongest evidence that doulas reduce cesarean section rates for pregnant women in the adult age category. More research must be conducted to confirm the differences in degree of benefit between the age groups.

abstract:
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity, often emerging in early childhood and impacting social, emotional, and academic development. Given the high heritability of ADHD, many parents – particularly mothers – of affected children also exhibit symptoms that may, in turn, influence their parenting behaviors. This study examined associations between maternal ADHD symptoms, parenting behaviors, and child behavioral outcomes. Eighty-eight mothers of children aged 4-6 were recruited via Prolific and completed the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS), the Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire (CECPAQ), and the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Results indicated that although more boys (67.5%) than girls (44.7%) were diagnosed with ADHD, symptom severity did not significantly differ by gender. Children diagnosed with ADHD showed significantly higher internalizing behaviors, t(87)=2.22, p=.029, but not externalizing behaviors. Maternal inattention was significantly associated with greater use of negative discipline, r(87)=.29, p=.01, though no meaningful associations emerged with warmth or positive discipline. Additionally, positive discipline was negatively correlated with children’s internalizing behaviors, r(87)=-.27, p=.01.

Findings suggest that maternal ADHD symptoms, particularly inattention, are linked to greater use of negative discipline, which may contribute to child behavioral difficulties. The gender gap in diagnoses, despite comparable symptom severity, further highlights potential diagnostic biases. The use of a community, rather than clinical, sample may have influenced parent-reported data and should be considered in future research.

According to previous research, Generation Z undergraduate students, or students born between 1997 and 2012, are experiencing unprecedented high levels of anxiety. Another study investigated whether anxiety is more strongly predicted by undergraduate students’ cognition and thought processes (internal factors) or the university environment (external factors), and whether these factors play an equal role. Defined as highly ranked universities with low acceptance rates, elite institutions may bolster anxiety levels due to the perceived environment, as suggested by Role Strain Theory. Alternatively, anxious students may be self-selecting into elite universities, as those with a high need for achievement and high avoidance goals experience more anxiety.

Participants within this study were undergraduate students who attended a wide range of institutions, each with varying degrees of selectivity. They completed measures of anxiety (state-trait, general), internal factors (goal orientation, fear of failure, and achievement motivation), and external factors (class and professor perceptions). Results suggested that internal factors, specifically fear of failure, were the strongest predictor of anxiety compared to external factors. There were no significant differences between selective, moderately selective, and less selective schools in overall anxiety when compared across three groups, but students at the most selective schools were surprisingly less anxious than students enrolled in moderate and less selective schools when those groups were combined. Altogether, the findings suggested that internal factors – goal orientation, fear of failure, and achievement motivation – are the largest determinants of undergraduate anxiety, compared to institutional selectivity and environmental perceptions.

Spelling to Communicate (S2C) is an increasingly visible motor-based communication method for minimally speaking autistic individuals, yet its scientific status remains unsettled. This review evaluates S2C’s theoretical claims, instructional framework, and empirical evidence within the broader context of motor function, language comprehension, and assessment limitations in minimally speaking autism. Research across fine motor skills, oromotor control, neural organization, and electrophysiological responses shows that motor differences can influence expressive behavior and that standard speech and motor dependent assessments often underestimate ability. These findings create plausible conditions for S2C’s rationale that expressive limitations may mask underlying competence. At the same time, current S2C-specific studies, which rely on small samples and unblinded observational designs, do not establish independent authorship or demonstrate that motor training yields reliable, self-generated communication. Anecdotal reports and media examples illustrate a wide range of real-world experiences but do not provide controlled evidence. This review integrates these domains to clarify where S2C’s assumptions align with existing research, where claims remain untested, and what methodological advances are needed. Establishing independent authorship, improving outcome measures, and defining appropriate target populations are essential steps toward determining whether S2C is a valid communication approach for minimally speaking individuals.

In the past few years, educators have been pushing for an integration of the arts into science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) learning to promote innovation and creativity in these fields. The present study explores the relation between creativity and STEM learning among young children in digital and non-digital contexts, and how creativity affects STEM engagement. Parent-child dyads consisting of one parent and one child aged 4-and-a-half to 5-years old participated in a repeated measures experiment during which they played with magnetic tiles, similar to blocks, and then with a coding application on a tablet. Levels of creativity during non-digital play, performance on the coding application and parent report of children’s STEM engagement are measured to better understand their relation. Results show that there may be a connection between creativity and STEM learning, but this relation is still unclear. This study will contribute to the development of STEM curriculum and its incorporation of creative activities in the preschool years.

abstract: Morocco is a fairly stable country, with parliamentary elections and limited political instability. When compared to neighbors such as Egypt and Tunisia, Morocco came out of the Arab Spring relatively unscathed. However, the Moroccan people remain unhappy with the economic state of their country. In a country of 34.9 million people, unemployment is at 10% and youth unemployment is at a staggering 27.5%, with female unemployment surpassing that number. The 42% of urban Moroccans who are unemployed have been protesting and voicing their discontent at the economic situation; experts call this a “ticking time bomb.” ³ This structural unemployment can be accredited to the education system’s rigid and increasingly obsolete curriculum, a rising population and the lack of private-sector job creation. Additionally, the unemployment rate is leading to an increase in inequality and is putting a strain on government social programs. Morocco is facing a great economic challenge, one that requires robust job creation and innovative solutions. However, the high unemployment rates and rising inequality cannot be overcome unless the government harnesses the talent and potential of Moroccan women.

abstract: What we know about the Mammoth Cave system stems from the 833 km of explored cave, but it is hypothesized that this represents only half of the total cave system. Many caves passages within this complex system are extremely hard and, in some cases, impossible to physically access. The independent water source feeding the Echo River Accessory Spring can be classified as one of these “impossible” caves to access. Mammoth Cave scientists have attempted to use a variety of different methods, such as dye-tracing, scuba diving, and even remotely operated vehicles, to access this water-filled cave passage, with no success. Difficulty in locating the water-filled cave passage feeding the Echo River Accessory Spring suggests that another approach is necessary. Electrical resistivity tomography allows us to model and “explore” caves tens of meters below the Earth’s surface without stepping foot inside. Using this technique, we imaged low-resistivity anomalies interpreted to be water-filled cave passages, which likely supply the Echo River Accessory Spring water. This result characterizes a previously undiscovered Mammoth Cave passage and could potentially extend the known extent of the total cave system. These findings will ultimately open up the possibility for further scientific advancements regarding the cave. We also anticipate that this result will allow for a better understanding of how water flows through the Mammoth Cave system and out through springs into the Green River, while also demonstrating the utility of ERT in subsurface karst terrain exploration.

abstract:
This project aims to discover new molecules from microbial extracts that prove toxic to C. elegans yet harmless to mammals...

One promising compound has been screened against C. elegans, and while the results seem to illustrate a sensitivity to the compound in traits such as mean time of flight (animal length), this may be an artifact of the assay because the brood size (animal fertility) seemed to increase with increasing drug concentration.

The question of man’s origin has plagued philosophers, scientists, and intellectuals alike for centuries. After Charles Darwin’s revolutionary Origin of Species (1859) and The Descent of Man (1871) were published, fossil discoveries became paramount in establishing the connection between humans and earlier life forms...

However, despite decades of progress, the absence of the ‘missing link’ between apes and humans confounded scientists. In 1891 Dutch paleoanthropologist and geologist Eugene Dubois discovered what was claimed to be the missing link in the Dutch East Indies. He dubbed the fossil he discovered in Trinil, Java “Java Man” (Pithecanthropus erectus). Java Man was later found to be a subspecies of Homo Erectus, but for a time debate raged regarding its place in human ancestry.

The American film industry is inextricably tied to the history of racism in the United States; thus, Black representation in film and T.V. has been a topic of rigorous academic and public debate. Most recently, that debate has circulated around the topic of “Black Trauma Porn” (BTP). Emerging on social media in 2016 during the Black Lives Matter movement, Black thinkers used the phrase “Black Trauma Porn” to articulate the nuanced complexities of the phenomenon, specifically sharing police brutality videos and the production of films and T.V. series with similar themes. Many piec­ es have received extreme backlash, and BTP became loaded with negative connotations, labeling the pieces as exploitative and harmful. However, as the phrase gained popularity, the analysis of these movies and T.V. shows became derivative and uncritical, instigating the need to investigate if the phrase properly articulates what authors were utilizing it for. To interrogate BTP, it is necessary to explain the impact of film on the spectator and engage the history of race in Hollywood in order to conclude that BTP is actually a modernist subgenre of Black horror. This conclusion is supported through an analysis of white versus Black horror as well as a deep-dive into what “trauma” and “porn” mean individually and within this context. Reframing and usurping the phrase BTP provides the beginning to a new framework for analyzing Black historical horror films and answering larger questions about Black representation in film and T.V.

Epistemic injustice, and testimonial injustice specifically, is a type of dis­ crimination that occurs when a person suffers a credibility deficit because of an identity-based prejudice. This is an issue that affects many marginalized groups and can have larger repercussions on one’s perception of self, loss of resources and opportunities, and continued mistreatment, both epistemically and non-epistemically. My project explores this phenomenon in relation to Asian/American women, which I identify to be an at-risk group for system­ atic, testimonial injustice. Through the course of this thesis, I discuss how stereotypes about Asian/Americans, and Asian/American women in partic­ ular, were created and how these stereotypes negatively impact the perceived credibility of Asian/Americans, both historically and currently. The goal of this is to problematize the dominant images of Asian/American women and to show how this idea is not informed by actual Asian/American women but by dominant and oppressive forces such as white supremacy, patriarchal power, and Western exceptionalism. Furthermore, I argue that testimonial injustice against Asian/American women can reproduce and maintain these negative images and that the discrediting of this group can lead to further, non-epistemic harms like physical and sexual violence. Because of this, how we conceptualize justice for Asian/American women socially and politically is deeply tied to epistemic justice, which serves as a method I discuss for overall resistance to violent powers.

This study will examine the power dynamics between undergraduate students and adult community members, and their effects on mediating these relation­ ships within the realm of university—community partnerships. More specifi­ cally, this paper explores a community engagement program categorized as an out-of-school learning initiative. This means that the partnership is between a university entity and an external organization, or in this case, several communi­ ty organizations. The relationships between undergraduate students and adult community members is an important dimension to investigate because it is vast­ ly understudied and consequential to the outcome of the partnership. Through the analysis of end-of-the-year surveys, Identity Journals, and Team Lead focus group transcripts, the data reveals the significant effects of preexisting content expertise, pre-planning meetings, and resource access. These observations led to my present research question: How do power dynamics mediate relationships between Team Leads (T.L.s) and Undergraduate Collaboratives (U.C.s) within Young People’s Race Power and Technology Project (YPRPT)?

This case study of YPRPT reveals the complexity of undergraduate and com­ munity member relationships within an organization bringing high schoolers, undergraduates (U.C.s), and community partners (T.L.s) together to investigate the impacts that technology has on marginalized groups of color through the cre­ ation of investigative documentaries. Successful interactions occurred when the intrapersonal skills of all facilitators were respected and valued, which was aided by interpersonal skills such as active listening and a shared sense of teamwork and purpose. The most cited interaction event mentioned was the collaborative method of planning sessions. These gave the facilitators time to get to know each other on both a personal and professional level. This gained knowledge then led to a sense of trust, limited due to time but still present and evident, and a division of responsibilities that supported the learning of the participants.

Ask the Oxford Encyclopedia of Theatre and Performance or a passerby in the lobby of Northwestern University’s performing arts center and the qual­ ifications seem consistent: If a teenage girl onstage is a significant character, then she is an ingénue. And if she is an ingénue, she is innocent, simple, a specific kind of “pretty,” and a host of other similar requirements.

What does it mean when this is the theatre’s prescription of what young womanhood looks like? How does it impact artists and audiences? Can we imagine an engagement with the canon that might embody young woman­ hood in a truthful, inclusive, and positively impactful way? These questions drove a four-part research process, consisting of investigation of published writing, discussion with an ensemble of my peers (eight fellow young women from N.U.’s theatre department), exploration with that ensemble via practice and performance of a selection of relevant repertoire, and audience surveys. While this project began out of my own frustrations from “within” the type — often seen for ingénue roles, they felt limiting — my findings underscored the extent to which type expectations often exclude many young women from these roles entirely, frequently with profound consequences. I ultimate­ ly found that traditional images of young womanhood (particularly, but not exclusively, in older texts) leave much to be desired in their impacts on both actors and audiences. However, a radically different, positive impact seems possible through contemporary texts which reimagine teenage girlhood onstage, and through reinventive interpretation, staging, and/or casting of more traditional works.

Orchestras are important cultural institutions and as such they are representations of greater socio—political movements. They often act as mirrors of political, social, and cultural landscapes, and reflect the greater values and beliefs within a given time. After the fall of the Berlin Wall, the greater themes of Germany during the Wendezeit were reflected in the activities of the orchestras, musical institutions, and concert program­ ming in the orchestras in Berlin and acted as representations of cultural politics during this transitional period. By examining three significant reunification concerts in Berlin between late 1989 and early 1990, I will explain the ways in which the orchestras in Berlin acted as a microcosm for the greater German society. Through these analyses, I will highlight the unequal preservation of cultural institutions in the former East Berlin and the Bundesrepublik and explain the resurgence of the ideals of the French Revolu­ tion and Germany as das Land der Dichter und Denker that is intertwined with it. I will illustrate the connections between the large presence of Beethoven’s music, the idea of the Gesamtkunstwerk, and the influence of figures such as Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Friedrich Schiller, and Karl Friedrich Schinkel on the curated image of the reunification concerts in Berlin. I will also question who controlled the narrative in this period of transition and who the collective audience was after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

Over the last decade, public schools have seen a dramatic rise in the use of visible school security measures, including metal detectors, security cameras, and security personnel (Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015). Although several studies have examined the impact of a school security presence on students’ academic outcomes, only a few studies have looked at how a security presence impacts school climate and student wellbeing, largely focus­ ing on quantitative analyses. The lack of more qualitative approaches that offer in-depth descriptions of students’ lived experiences limits the scope of assessments examining school security presences. The present study seeks to fill these gaps by examining the relationship between school security and school climate through the lens of student wellbeing. A survey was completed by 97 Northwestern first-year students, assessing their high school’s climate with or without a school security presence. Afterward, 10 students were selected for follow-up interviews. The semi-structured interviews con­ sisted of items related to dimensions of school climate and adolescent wellbeing, and all selected interviewees graduated from a high school with a security presence. Findings of the study included the impact of school violence on a student’s relationship with their school’s security and administration and its consequences for school climate and student wellbeing; direct impacts of school security on student wellbeing; how different security types elicit different perceptions in students; how student identity impacts the relation­ ship between a student and their school’s security presence; and how a lack of adequate support affects student perception of school climate and student wellbeing.

BeReal grew rapidly in popularity throughout 2022. Created as a response to social media platforms where idealized images and higher usage are encouraged, BeReal takes a different approach. Valuing authenticity, BeReal asks users to post a daily front and back-facing picture within a random two-minute time slot and provides a short daily feed of BeReals from friends. In an online survey, U.S. college students 18-23 years old were studied in two groups: BeReal users (n = 100) and non-BeReal users (n =100). Both groups completed questions on perception and usage of different social media platforms and anxiety, public self-consciousness, fear of missing out, and authenticity scales. BeReal users were asked additional questions to observe trends in how people use and perceive BeReal, determine the extent to which BeReal usage moderates the relationship between total time spent on social media and anxiety, and examine whether inauthentic BeReal behaviors are correlated with greater anxiety, self-consciousness, fear of missing out, and inauthenticity. Results show that BeReal usage did not significantly mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, fear of missing out, public self-conscious­ ness, and authenticity. The average user posted 78% of the time, posted late 52% of the time, and retook their BeReal at least once 37% of the time before posting. While the app was designed to promote authenticity by keeping users accountable, actual users were more forgiving with these inauthentic behaviors, with the median accepted late post of 10 hours late and the median accepted number of retakes being three. We also found that the percentage of late posts had a negative public correlation with anxiety, and the percentage of skipped posts had a positive correlation with public self-consciousness.

Media accounts report that the COVID-19 pandemic and 2020 Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement disproportionately affected Black communities and businesses, amplifying already- existing racial health and economic disparities. Black-owned small businesses experienced significant indirect and direct economic damages in Chicago, Illinois, and research literature is now striving to provide analyses of Black business owners’ experiences in 2020. The present study uses quantitative and qualitative data analyses to discern the impact of 2020 crises on small businesses in Englewood, Chicago. The study examined foot traffic data from cell-phone records to identify business visitation patterns relative to the March 21 Illinois stay-at-home order and the commencement of BLM protests after the murder of George Floyd on May 25. After both March 21 and May 25, there were statistically significant changes in foot traffic in majority-Black neighborhoods as compared to majority-non-Black neighborhoods. The research elucidated the complexity of the mechanisms by which COVID-19 and BLM activities disproportionately influenced Black communities through semi-structured interviews with Black-identifying small business owners (n=8) in Englewood. The study participants detailed their evolving perceptions of policing in Englewood after looting in June, concern for employee well-being in the pandemic, and complex grant application processes throughout 2020. Business owners were motivated to keep their firms open to support their families, promote values benefitting Englewood residents, and refute stereotypes about Englewood itself. This project provides insight into the range of experiences Black entrepreneurs in Englewood have faced in 2020 and suggests ways that policy responses might usefully support their survival and success.

abstract: Energy poverty can be understood as the inability or difficulty of a household to meet their basic energy needs. While the condition is already widespread across Europe, it will likely worsen in the near future, as average temperatures increase due to climate change and there becomes a greater need for heating and/or cooling. The present study addresses the gap in research in this area by using Eurostat data on energy poverty and changes in heating degree-days (HDD) and cooling degree-days (CDD) across the 28 European Union (EU) Member States from 2004–2019. These metrics are then used to create a composite indicator of energy poverty based on a household’s inability to keep warm, pay utility bills on time, and the presence of damp, leakage, or rot in the home. The results indicate that an increase in the number of days in which air conditioning is needed to be comfortable significantly increases the share of energy-poor households, but there is no significant association with HDD. Additionally, a comprehensive analysis of temporal and macroeconomic trends shows that energy poverty is severely unevenly distributed across the Member States and that both climate change and the ongoing energy transition will likely exacerbate these inequalities. Thus, policy implications include increasing general awareness of the phenomenon and implementing country-specific policies that directly address energy poverty in the context of a changing climate, especially in Southern and Eastern European EU countries.

Under the double oppression of the U.S.’ neocolonial occupation and the South Korean state’s neo-Confucian patriarchy, Korean women experience an alienation from their own bodies, becoming objects of sexual production. Although this is an issue that is written about passionately within the banmi, or anti-American literary genre, it is an issue that is often categorized under the greater narrative of national liberation from U.S. forces. This male-centered utilization of female suffering is unfortunately also a part of South Korea’s double colonialism.

Oh Jung-Hee’s Junggugingeori, a novella that delivers its anti-American criticism indirectly through metaphors and juxtaposition, is uninterested in metaphorizing the female experience to merely become a pawn in the drive towards a male-centered decolonization. Instead, Junggugingeori simultaneously criticizes the U.S. and the South Korean state through the depiction of female characters’ suffering and resistance against the double oppression of patriarchy and neocolonialism, partaking in the banmi literary movement without offering the female experience up for male exploitation.

The purpose of this project is to examine how Junggugingeori portrays its protag- onists’ individual bodily resistance to double colonialism. I propose that Oh portrays resistance against the joint forces of patriarchy and U.S. neocolonial oppression through the juxtaposition of the narrator’s witnessing of the sexualized violence that the adult women in her life are forced to suffer with her own private and seemingly unrelated physical resistance against her body.

abstract: What explains Indian American attitudes towards Hindu nationalism? Following the election of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in 2014, Hindutva, or Hindu nationalism, has become a potent political force in India. In the Indian diaspora, particularly in the United States, the past decade has seen an increase in public activity related to Hindu nationalism. From the World Hindu Congress in Chicago to President Trump and Prime Minister Modi’s massive joint rally in Texas to demonstrations against Hindu nationalist citizenship laws in India, Indian Americans are now more vocal than ever about politics in India. This study employs regression analysis to identify key predictors of Hindu nationalism among Indian Americans. Religious identity and behavior, Islamophobia, and certain benchmarks of assimilation emerge as statistically significant. Little empirical work has been conducted on the subject of Hindu nationalism in the United States, especially after the ascendance of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in 2014. As one of the first surveys of Indian Americans focused on Hindu nationalism, this work evaluates the existing theoretical explanations for the phenomenon and helps set the agenda for future research. Furthermore, this study puts forth a method for quantitatively measuring attitudes towards Hindu nationalism: the index of Hindu nationalist sentiment.

The following paper seeks to explore and discover how the tools and resources that actors gain throughout their training are applicable to vocations outside of just performing and in the process of everyday life. By conducting interviews with current Northwestern students, current and former Northwestern acting professors, as well as Northwestern alumni who are at the pinnacle of their fields in both the entertainment industry and professions outside of this particular industry, I use anecdotes and qualitative applications to dive into the substance, and not just the form, of acting — in short, this paper will share how techniques and skills related to the entertainment industry are crucial to more than just the actor. Furthermore, I argue that being an actor is akin to being a scientist and that the process an actor undergoes in preparing to play a role is a process one should try to implement in their own walk of life.

Gender-based violence (GBV) is a prevalent issue on a global scale, but the effects of such violence upon Asian/Asian American communities in the United States is compounded by their immigrant, refugee, and/or other historically marginalized identities. While current literature recognizes GBV as a public health issue of equity and social justice, anthropology closely examines the asymmetry of power by informing a holistic view of local contexts. The research examines the perspectives of Asian-identifying frontline workers within domestic violence agencies and multi-service organizations in Chicagoland. Frontline workers, such as social workers and legal advocates, play a pivotal role in serving survivors and offering intimate local-level knowledge. Feminist ethnography grounded in Asian American Critical Race Theory (AsianCrit) guided data collection and analysis. Ethnographic fieldwork at a local domestic violence agency for six (6) weeks was conducted and fourteen (14) key informant interviews with frontline workers from five (5) non- profits across Chicagoland took place. The analysis demonstrates that their labor as influenced by personal life histories, or “radical caring,” provides agency to survivors on the individual, relationship, community, and societal levels, aligning with the WHO Socio-Ecological Framework for Violence Prevention. The positionality of frontline workers is crucial in eradicating gender-based violence and resisting the structural violence affecting all female and non-binary people of color. Highlighting the advocacy of frontline workers broadens interdisciplinary understandings of gender-based violence in anthropology, public health, critical race studies, and other social science disciplines.

abstract: This paper investigates the historical impacts of water pollution on downstream communities along the Mississippi River during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. As industrialization and urbanization intensified, urban centers and industries along the river increasingly discharged untreated pollutants into the water, thereby transforming the river from a residential amenity into a significant disamenity. Drawing from historical surveys and census data, this study examines how changes in pollution levels influenced population shifts in downstream counties relative to their upstream counterparts. I found that increased levels of upstream pollution had significant and economically meaningful effects on downstream populations, with pollution levels correlating negatively with population sizes. These findings are robust across a range of pollution specifications. Furthermore, I found that the impact of upstream pollution became more severe between 1880 and 1900 before declining from 1910 onwards. I hypothesize that the intercity effects of upstream pollution contributed to the urban mortality penalty before declining in the early 20th century as cities began adopting modern water purification technologies to mitigate the adverse effects of pollution and water-borne diseases. This paper contributes to the broader economic discourse on environmental externalities and neighborhood amenities by detailing the intercity effects of water pollution.

In this study, we employ a conjoint analysis to assess what factors influence the likelihood of male and female candidates being perceived as leaders. In particular, we consider the influence of agency and communality stereotypes in terms of personality, emotionality, and parental status. Participants evaluated a set of fictitious employee profiles of a consulting firm, selecting which employees they considered most deserving of being promoted to managers. Participant evaluations were then analyzed to determine the relative importance of eight study attributes in influencing the probability of managerial promotion (i.e., leadership selection). In this paper, we discuss two of our main findings. First, when emotional control is described as fair, female candidates are less likely than male candidates to be chosen as leaders. Second, certain agentic female leaders benefit from being described as mothers: bossy, but not ambitious, female candidates are more likely to be chosen as leaders when described as having children compared to when described as childless.

State merit-based scholarships are a large source of funding for many college students, and the effects of this aid on families, students, and states’ economies is a topic of continued interest and research. There are 22 states with merit aid programs, and because eligibility includes graduating from an in-state high school, students and parents in some states can depend on this aid while others cannot. I use this variation, documented by the InforeED State Financial Aid Dataset, together with survey data on people’s decisions to save for college, provided by the National Financial Capability Survey, to assess the effect of merit aid programs on college savings. I find mixed evidence, some suggesting that living in a state with a merit aid program meaningfully decreases the likelihood of saving for college, and some suggesting that it has no effect. I assess whether the scholarships change the amount parents save using the College Savings Plan Network data on 529 accounts. My results are inconclusive, and I propose redoing my analysis with the Survey of Consumer Finances confidential dataset. My analysis is limited by the fact that data sets containing both a measure of college savings and the state of residence are difficult to obtain and/or to use because of the structure of the available data. The purpose of this paper is, in addition to quantifying the effect of scholarships on savings, to describe the potential data sources, limitations, and possible strategies, to inform future related work.

When the United States (U.S.) entered World War II in 1942, 12,000 men refused uniformed service through the draft. These conscientious objectors (C.O.s) were, however, willing to perform alternative service. This project focuses on the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, which was conducted between 1944 and 1945 at the University of Minnesota’s Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene and used C.O.s as volunteer human subjects. In conducting the experiment, the doctors (led by Ancel Keys) and subjects hoped to understand the biological and psychological effects of starvation and illuminate best practices to nourish the starving populations of Europe after World War II. In order to accomplish these aims, the 36 C.O.s under- went a control period of three months, a systematic semistarvation of six months, and a rehabilitation period of three months. This project integrates the Minnesota Experiment with the social and political landscapes of an America engaged in total war, bridging a gap between scholarship that discusses the experiment as a micro- history and broader scholarships of World War II that mention it only in passing. It does so by demonstrating and analyzing the parallels between specific groups in the experiment and specific groups in the military, showing how the character of total war became part of an experiment that was defined by its separation from combat and military institutions. In demonstrating these parallels and contextualizing the experiment in the climate of total war, the Minnesota Starvation Experiment emerges as both extraordinary and unprecedented while also deeply ordinary in the context of its own time.

While global economic growth rises, international poverty also continues to increase. From 2022-2023, the population living below the international poverty line increased by 4%, now estimated at 31.4% of the global population. Indeed, poverty is multidimensional, and the multilateral allocation of resources is continuously reevaluated at the household-level. Founded around this guiding principle, alongside modern development theory on poverty traps (Duflo’s “poor but neoclassical”), it is hypothesized that the regular occurrence of economic shocks—e.g. natural disasters, global pandemics, and political, ethnic, and religious conflicts— keep poor households poor by forcing such households to respond by reducing caloric intake, limiting cognitive development and long-term health. We find that short- and long-term effects differ with respect to these outcomes. In particular, significant short-term decreases in nutritional status are found, prominently guided by age-effects, as well as significantly lower assessed cognitive ability. While some long-term differences are reported with regard to physical activities of daily life, more studies must be done in this area to confirm relevance and results.

Grief, an omnipresent human experience, has been analyzed throughout time through various models and lenses in order to make sense of the abstract concept. ‘Grief Unmasked’ answers the question, “How can the use of masquerade as an embodied practice manifest and express the various experiences of grief?” through eight masquerade masks. In order, the masks are titled: “Shock,” “Denial,” “Guilt,” “Anger,” “Bargaining,” “Depression,” “Reconstruction,” and “Acceptance.” Each mask draws on interdisciplinary perspectives from psychology, religion, and artistic symbolism to create an experience that is more evocative and individualized than scholarly research on grief.

abstract: We attempted to determine the causal effect of the 1993 European Union and 1998 United States copyright term extensions on creative productivity as measured by movie production in Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, and the United States, using a novel methodology which exploits the transnational nature of modern copyright law to generate a source of exogenous variation. This would extend the results of Giorcelli and Moser (2020), which showed that the introduction of copyright had a positive causal effect on creative productivity. However, we were unable to find a pair of countries which satisfied our tests for parallel pre-treatment trends. As such, we generated no results about the effect of treatment, as the difference-in-differences design relies on the assumption of parallel trends.
